prompt: Find the k-th largest element in an unsorted array of up to 10⁵ numbers.
why: Keep a min-heap of size k; its top is the answer. O(n log k).
trap: Sorting works in O(n log n). Quickselect is faster on average, but the heap is the reliable pattern.

prompt: Return the k most frequent words in a document, ties broken alphabetically.
why: Count with a hashmap, then keep the top k with a heap.
trap: The hashmap counts, but it doesn't rank. You still need the top-k step.

prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
why: A min-heap holds the current head of each list. Pop the smallest, push its successor.
trap: Two pointers merges two lists. With k lists you need a fast “which head is smallest?”, which is a heap.

prompt: Numbers arrive one at a time. After each arrival, report the median of everything seen so far.
why: Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced.
trap: Re-sorting on every arrival is O(n log n) per query.

prompt: Given a list of points on a plane, return the k closest to the origin.
why: Max-heap of size k on distance; evict the farthest when it overflows.
trap: “Closest” isn't BFS. There's no graph, only distances.

prompt: Given meeting start and end times, find the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two meetings overlap in the same room.
why: Sort by start. A min-heap of end times: reuse a room when the earliest end ≤ the next start.
trap: It's an intervals problem, but the heap of end times answers “is any room free yet?”

prompt: Join n ropes into one. Joining two ropes costs their combined length. Find the minimum total cost.
why: Always join the two shortest: pop two from a min-heap, push the sum back.
trap: Sorting once isn't enough. Joined ropes re-enter the pool and must be re-ranked.

prompt: Rearrange a string so that no two adjacent characters are the same, or report that it's impossible.
tells: no two adjacent characters are the same
why: Greedy: place the most frequent remaining character that isn't the one just placed. A max-heap by count.
trap: It looks like a string-window problem, but it's “repeatedly take the most frequent”.

prompt: Numbers arrive one at a time. After each, report the 3rd largest number seen so far.
why: Keep a min-heap of size 3; its top is the answer after every insert.
trap: Re-sorting after every arrival is O(n log n) each time.

prompt: Tasks arrive at given times with given durations. A single CPU always runs the available task with the shortest duration next. Output the order.
tells: always runs the available task with the shortest duration next
why: Sort by arrival, push arrived tasks into a min-heap by duration, pop one at a time.
trap: It's a greedy rule, but you need a heap to apply it fast.

prompt: From a list of workers with costs, pick the k cheapest repeatedly as the list keeps growing with new applicants.
why: A heap keeps the cheapest available on top as items arrive, without re-sorting.
trap: Sorting once is fine for a fixed list; a growing one is what a heap is for.
